tips.li: Sleeping on the ground or outside gives a mood penalty every single night. A simple bed in a room is one of the cheapest mood boosts in the game.
Barracks are fine early on, but each colonist in one gets a mood penalty. Small private bedrooms, even 3×4, beat a big shared room.
A bedroom's impressiveness gives a mood bonus or penalty every morning. Floors, a bit of art and good furniture add up quickly.
Assign beds yourself in the bed's Owner tab, so couples share and loners get their own rooms.
Everyone in a barracks shares one impressiveness score, so one big, clean, decorated barracks can beat several plain bedrooms.
A bedroom stops counting as one if it holds a medical or prisoner bed, or more than one bed nobody owns.
Aim for a bedroom space of 25 or more: a 5x5 room with a bed, dresser and end table comes to about 31.
Outdoor crops stop growing once the average temperature falls below about 6°C. Everything you'll eat in winter has to be harvested, hunted or bought before then.
A colonist eats about 1.6 nutrition a day. Rice grows fastest, potatoes tolerate poor soil, and corn stores well but grows slowly.
Hunting, trading and fishing all fill gaps. Wild animals often leave the map in winter, so hunt before the cold sets in.
Food in a cold room lasts much longer. Below 0°C most food stops rotting entirely.
A simple meal rots in 4 days without cold storage; pemmican keeps 70 days, corn 60, rice 40, potatoes 30.
Plants rest at night, so real growing time is about 1.85 times what a crop's info card says.
A colonist eats about 1.8 simple meals a day: a 15-day winter needs roughly 27 meals each.
Plants start dying below -10 °C. When frost is coming, harvest anything ripe enough to give a yield.
Rotting food is wasted work. A freezer (a closed room cooled below 0°C) stops most spoilage cold.
Coolers push heat out one side and cold in the other. Put them in a wall with the hot side facing outside, and use a double door to keep the cold in.
Without cooling you can still preserve food: pemmican and other preserved foods last far longer than raw crops or meat.
Food stops rotting at 0 °C and below. Between 0 and 10 °C it only rots more slowly.
Set two coolers a little apart, for example -5 °C and -10 °C, so a door left open doesn't thaw the room.
Passive coolers can't go below 17 °C. They keep people comfortable but can't keep food fresh.
Hypothermia and heatstroke kill quietly. Check each colonist's comfortable temperature range on their Gear tab.
Thick walls and closed doors hold heat. A heat source in a small room goes much further than one in a big hall.
Warm clothes count: parkas and tribalwear widen the range a colonist can work in comfortably.
In heat waves, an unroofed area or a room dug into a mountain can be noticeably cooler.
A cold snap drops temperatures by about 20 °C for 1.5 to 3.5 days; a heat wave adds up to 17 °C. Both pass, if you're ready.
Workbenches in rooms colder than 10 °C or hotter than 35 °C work noticeably slower.
Raids scale with colony wealth. Getting richer without getting stronger is the classic mid-game trap.
Cover matters more than numbers. Colonists behind sandbags or walls take far less damage than ones standing in the open.
Funnel attackers through a narrow approach covered by your shooters (and traps), so you choose where the fight happens.
Wealth includes everything: stockpiles, buildings, even art. Selling or using up surplus items lowers raid size.
This is a rough estimate: it counts fighters, weapons, turrets, traps and cover, not how clever your layout is.
Cover matters: walls, rock and doors give up to 75% cover, sandbags and barricades 55%, trees only 25%.
Traps trigger every time for raiders and manhunters, and only about once in 200 crossings for your own people.
Raids grow with your wealth and your colonists. Silver and art in a box count against you just as much as anything else.
Untreated wounds get infected. A doctor and some medicine turn a deadly wound into a few days of bed rest.
Medical beds in a clean room improve tend quality and lower infection chance. Clean floors matter more than you'd think.
Healroot can be grown for herbal medicine. It's weaker than industrial medicine, but far better than nothing.
Medicine potency: herbal 60%, industrial 100%, glitterworld 160%. Treating with no medicine at all is only 30%.
Hospital beds improve tend quality and immunity gain; a vitals monitor raises surgery success further.
Solar and wind are free but unreliable: night, calm days and eclipses all happen. Batteries smooth it out.
Solar flares shut down all electricity for a while. Keep important things (like freezers) well insulated so they ride it out.
Batteries can explode during rain, or catch fire from zzzt events. Keep them roofed, and away from things that burn.
Ordinary conduits and unroofed batteries can short out and start fires; hidden conduits and roofed batteries can't.
A solar flare lasts only a few hours but kills everything electric. Wood-fueled stoves and smithies keep working through it.
Colonists get bored of the same recreation. Several different kinds (social, gaming, cerebral and so on) keep their recreation need full.
As the colony gets richer, expectations rise and colonists want more variety.
A dedicated rec room with a few different games is one of the best long-term mood investments.
A full recreation need gives up to +10 mood; below 30% it starts to hurt, and below 15% it hurts a lot.
Every kind of recreation wears thin with use. Variety keeps it working.
Eating without a table gives a mood penalty at every meal. A table and chairs pay for themselves almost immediately.
An impressive dining room gives a mood bonus after every meal, and everyone eats three times a day.
Eating without a table costs 3 mood, every meal, for everyone.
Fine meals give +5 mood and lavish meals +12, from the same ingredients a good cook already has.
Below the break threshold colonists can snap: binges, sad wanders, or worse. Fix the biggest negative thought first.
Quick mood fixes: a good meal, recreation time, a nicer bedroom, a party, or simply giving someone a break from hard work.
Check the Needs tab: each thought shows exactly how much it moves mood, so you can see what matters most.
After a mental break a colonist gets Catharsis, a big mood boost for 3 days. It's a safety net, not a plan.
A body lying where people walk costs 4 mood each time someone sees it, 6 if it's rotting.
Low expectations are free mood: +30 in a poor colony, shrinking in steps as wealth grows.
A job nobody is assigned to never happens. Check the Work tab after every new recruit or loss.
Colonists with a passion for a skill learn it faster and enjoy the work. Put people where their flames are.
One or two hours of recreation in the schedule each day keeps tempers in check.
Most items slowly fall apart when left outside under the open sky. A roofed stockpile stops that.
Shelves stack several items per cell and keep them off the floor, so they don't deteriorate.
An idle research bench is wasted time. Even a slow project moves the colony forward.
The council suggests projects that fit your colony's era first. You can always choose your own on the Research tab.
Electricity costs 1,600 research (3,200 for a tribal start). It opens batteries, coolers, hydroponics and firefoam.
Ideas aren't problems, just directions you could take once the basics are covered.
A colony that only survives burns out. Comfort, beauty and purpose keep colonists going through the bad times.
